paragraphs: This report sets out what the first season of the survey found along the lower Ouse. Volunteers walked the banks every fortnight and took measurements of depth, colour and temperature at twelve fixed sites between York and Goole.

The work was planned with the Yorkshire water trust and with local schools. A wellknown problem with surveys of this kind is that the sites change between visits, so each one was marked with a numbered post. Jean-Paul Martin, who led the first walks, chose places where the bank was firm and the water was clearer than in the town centre, so that readings could be compared over the season.
• Counts of fish, birds and insects seen along both riverbanks at each site
• Notes on bank erosion after floods

The samples were tested within a day of being taken. Where a test could not be run in time, the sample was left out rather than estimated, and the lower reaches were affected most, because the boats that carry the samples upstream run only twice a week.
Depth changed little over the summer, except after the storms of late August, when the river rose by more than a metre in two days.
Temperature followed the air, rising from 9 to 19 degrees between May and July and falling again in September.
Colour readings were the least reliable part of the work. Most volunteers2 found it hard to match the water against the printed chart in bright sunlight.
2 Two of the twelve volunteers used tablets instead.

This report sets out what the first season of the

Paul Martin, who led the first walks, chose places

clearer than in the town centre, so that readings

• Water samples from twelve sites
• Counts of fish, birds and insects seen along both
riverbanks at each site

The samples were tested within a day of being
taken. Where a test could not be run in time, the
sample was left out rather than estimated, and the

samples upstream run only twice a week.
